strengths: Addresses practical and important problem of data-efficient humanoid robot learning with real-world validation on LimX Ohi robot
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with systematic ablation studies examining training time proportion, data proportion, and different SRL method choices
Well-structured methodology with clear formulation; intuitive use of contrastive learning between proprioceptive and privileged states
Provides actionable insights about when SRL helps (important for motion imitation, less critical for velocity tracking) with quantitative evidence
SRL4Humanoid framework contribution unifying multiple SRL implementations that could benefit the community
Computational efficiency analysis demonstrates feasibility of SRL methods with minimal overhead
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing contrastive learning techniques to robot domain rather than introducing fundamentally new methods
Modest empirical improvements, especially for velocity tracking where differences between PvP and PPO+SPR/SimSiam are small; final performance gains are incremental
Real-world validation is mostly qualitative (Figure 11 shows poses) without quantitative metrics comparing PvP vs baselines on actual robot; no real-world ablations
Narrow experimental scope with only 2 tasks and 1 robot platform; generalizability claims are overstated
Insufficient baseline comparisons: limited to PPO+SRL variants with no comparison to other state-of-the-art humanoid control methods (diffusion policies, transformers, behavior cloning)
Weak theoretical justification for why contrastive learning is specifically superior to other auxiliary losses for leveraging privileged information
Unresolved stability issues evident in training collapse (Figure 10) when applying SRL to value encoder; interval update mechanism (Eq. 6) lacks principled justification

Missing critical ablations: no analysis of contrastive loss design choices, scaling with privileged information dimensionality, or failure modes; inconsistent VAE underperformance not adequately explained
Important experimental details and hyperparameter search methodology relegated to appendices; unclear if all methods received uniform tuning; code availability not confirmed at submission
Ad-hoc design choices without principled justification (e.g., zero-masking operation in Eq. 2, why negative cosine similarity, scheduling strategy for SRL contribution)

strengths: Addresses practical problem of data-efficient humanoid WBC, which is relevant and challenging
SRL4Humanoid framework provides useful modular implementations of multiple SRL methods for community use
Systematic experimental design with 6 research questions and corresponding ablation studies
Includes real robot validation on LimX Oii humanoid, not just simulation
Generally clear presentation with informative figures and comprehensive appendices
Reasonable core idea of leveraging complementarity between proprioceptive and privileged states
weaknesses: Evaluation severely limited: only 2 tasks and 1 robot platform insufficient for claiming general data-efficiency improvements across humanoid WBC

Weak baselines: comparisons only against SRL variants with same PPO backbone; missing comparisons with model-based RL, other privileged information approaches, data augmentation, and other data-efficient methods
Modest and potentially insignificant improvements: 20-30% convergence speedup shown in Figures 5-6, overlapping confidence intervals in several cases, no statistical significance testing reported

Limited algorithmic novelty: core contribution simply combines well-established privileged information and contrastive learning techniques; no theoretical justification for why this combination is optimal

Zero-masking methodology (Eq. 2) poorly justified: assumes privileged information is only missing proprioceptive features, with no ablation against alternative designs for creating privileged information

Minimal real-world validation: Section 5.2.6 'real-world evaluation' is actually MuJoCo simulation configured for real-world conditions, not actual deployment; Figure 11 shows only qualitative results

Hyperparameter tuning concerns: different hyperparameters optimized for each method (Appendix C) without transparent reporting of effort parity; improvements could reflect superior tuning rather than algorithmic superiority
Incomplete ablations: Figure 9 shows minimal data proportion effects without explanation; Figure 8 shows confusing training time results; SRL encoder location only tested on one task
Statistical rigor lacking: no p-values, significance tests, or rigorous confidence intervals; claimed advantages may not be statistically significant
Insufficient novelty in loss formulation (Eq. 4): uses standard negative cosine similarity with no ablation justifying this choice over alternatives
Missing failure case analysis and insights: no discussion of when PvP helps vs. hurts, or task characteristics determining SRL utility

strengths: Real-world hardware validation: The paper demonstrates actual deployment on LimX Obi humanoid robot with motion imitation capability, which is rare and valuable for grounding the approach in practical scenarios

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Systematic ablations addressing six research questions (Q1-Q6) covering training time, data efficiency, encoder selection, computational cost, and real-world performance
Modular, reusable framework: SRL4Humanoid provides implementations of multiple state representation learning methods with unified interfaces, potentially benefiting the broader research community
Clear methodology and presentation: Well-structured paper with effective architecture diagrams, detailed algorithms, and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility

Practical insights: Identifies actionable findings including importance of careful update interval selection (Eq. 6), limitations of simple noise-based augmentation, task-dependent SRL effectiveness, and computational efficiency gains via GPU implementation
Addresses practical problem: Tackles genuine sample efficiency challenge in humanoid robot learning with a pragmatic multi-component approach
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution combines existing techniques (contrastive learning, privileged learning, state representation learning) without introducing fundamentally new mechanisms; zero-masking (Eq. 2) and architecture are straightforward applications of known ideas

Modest and inconsistent performance improvements: Gains over baselines are incremental; on motion imitation task (Figure 5), curves for PPO+SPR, PPO+SimSiam, and PPO+PvP substantially overlap; no statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported across results

Insufficient justification for design choices: Claim of 'intrinsic complementarity' between proprioceptive and privileged states lacks formal justification; why contrastive learning is superior to simpler alternatives (auxiliary losses, behavior cloning) is not rigorously motivated; interval update mechanism (Eq. 6) appears empirically motivated rather than principled

Narrow evaluation scope: Only two tasks on a single robot platform; no comparison with alternative privileged learning approaches; real-world validation only demonstrates functionality, not quantitative performance superiority versus baselines on hardware

Inadequate analysis of failure modes and task-dependent effectiveness: Figure 8-10 show SRL can degrade performance but lack deep investigation; motion imitation shows much smaller improvements than velocity tracking without principled explanation; unclear when practitioners should apply this versus simpler baselines

Incomplete sim-to-real gap analysis: While real-world validation is appreciated, only visual inspection provided (Figure 11); no quantitative comparison of sim-trained versus real-trained policies; unclear how privileged information access during deployment affects results

Experimental methodological concerns: Gaussian noise masking strategy appears ad-hoc with insufficient justification; fixed network architectures with no ablation on design choices; hyperparameter tuning procedures differ across SRL methods (Appendix C) complicating fair comparison; data augmentation operations in baselines incompletely discussed

strengths: Addresses important practical problem in humanoid robot learning with a well-motivated approach combining privileged information and contrastive learning

Comprehensive experimental validation including systematic ablation studies, simulation experiments on velocity tracking and motion imitation tasks, and real-robot demonstrations on the LimX Oii humanoid
SRL4Humanoid framework is a valuable open-source contribution providing high-quality, modular implementations of multiple SRL methods, beneficial for the research community
Thorough analysis of different factors affecting learning (training time proportion, data proportion, update intervals, weighting coefficients) offering practical insights
Includes real-world robot experiments beyond simulation, demonstrating practical applicability and motion imitation capabilities on actual hardware
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core idea is a relatively straightforward combination of existing concepts (privileged states + contrastive learning) without significant methodological innovations

Mixed and inconsistent experimental results: PvP shows clear improvements on velocity tracking but modest/inconsistent gains on motion imitation; VAE sometimes matches or exceeds PvP, and the paper inadequately explains these discrepancies or their implications for task generalization

Real-robot validation is primarily qualitative (visual demonstrations in Figure 11) without quantitative comparisons between methods on actual hardware, undermining claims about practical effectiveness

Insufficient theoretical justification: lack of rigorous analysis for why PvP should work, the 'intrinsic complementarity' claim needs deeper support, and design choices (e.g., Eq. 4 formulation, privileged state for value encoder) lack clear motivation

Narrow task evaluation: experiments limited to relatively simple, constrained scenarios (flat-terrain velocity tracking, pre-recorded motion imitation); acknowledged limitations with terrain variation and external disturbances suggest limited scope

Incomplete baseline comparisons: only compared against vanilla PPO + SRL methods; missing comparisons with recent data-efficient RL approaches, model-based methods, other privileged information techniques, or state-of-the-art humanoid control methods

Unclear design choices and justifications: zero-masking operation, hyperparameter selections appear arbitrary, and the scheduling mechanism (Eq. 6) seems ad-hoc; some design rationales only explained post-hoc

Statistical rigor concerns: unclear number of random seeds, some reported improvements appear within standard deviation ranges, and limited discussion of statistical significance despite shown error bars

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with systematic ablation studies investigating training time proportion, data proportion, and SRL method selection
Includes real-world validation on LinX Oii humanoid robot, moving beyond pure simulation
Practical contribution of SRL4Humanoid framework providing modular implementations of multiple SRL methods
Well-motivated problem addressing genuine challenges in humanoid robot learning with partial observability
Clear methodology with algorithm descriptions and reproducibility efforts (code availability mentioned)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: privileged information for RL and contrastive learning are well-established techniques; combining them is incremental application rather than fundamental advance

Modest and inconsistent empirical improvements: velocity tracking task shows marginal gains, and acknowledged issue that 'SRL loss does not always have positive influence and can sometimes degrade learning efficiency'
Insufficient real-world validation: limited to qualitative visual demonstrations (Figure 11) with no quantitative sim-to-real performance benchmarking

Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing recent state-of-the-art humanoid control methods and other privileged information approaches; TSD comparison shows competitive/better performance in several cases (Figures 13-15)

Inadequate justification of design choices: zero-masking operation lacks theoretical grounding; high sensitivity to hyperparameters (λ in Figure 17, update intervals) with limited principled selection guidance
Limited scope and generalization: tested only on single robot morphology (LinX Oii), two task types; no analysis of applicability to other humanoid designs
Presentation issues: dense notation, hard-to-read figures with overlapping lines, grammatical errors; relationship between components unclear
Missing critical ablations: no systematic comparison of contrastive vs. reconstruction-based SRL; no privileged learning vs. data augmentation comparison

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with systematic ablations examining key design choices (training proportion, data proportion, component placement) across two complementary tasks
Practical SRL4Humanoid framework providing modular, high-quality implementations of representative state representation learning methods with promised code release
Real-world validation on LimX Oii humanoid robot hardware demonstrates practical applicability beyond simulation, addressing sim-to-real challenges
Clear problem motivation and well-designed architecture effectively leveraging intrinsic complementarity between proprioceptive and privileged states without hand-crafted data augmentation
Rigorous baseline selection comparing against established SRL methods (SimSiam, SPR, VAE) rather than ad-hoc comparisons, with careful experimental setup ensuring fair evaluation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution reduces to combining existing SRL methods with standard weighted loss (Eq. 4-5); zero-masking operation is straightforward; primarily engineering contribution rather than fundamental innovation

Modest empirical improvements often within error margins: velocity tracking shows marginal gains over VAE, motion imitation improvements are minimal, and curves overlap substantially without statistical significance testing

Insufficient theoretical justification for why contrastive learning on privileged states improves policy learning; missing direct comparison with privileged state supervision and representation quality analysis

Narrow experimental scope limited to single humanoid robot and two related trajectory-tracking tasks; generalization to other morphologies, manipulation tasks, or complex long-horizon behaviors unclear

Incomplete real-world evaluation with only qualitative motion results (Figure 11) lacking quantitative metrics; no systematic sim-to-real transfer analysis or comparison of actual real-world performance improvements
Critical ablation deferred to appendix: teacher-student distillation (Figures 13-14) sometimes matches or exceeds PvP performance, questioning necessity of main contribution
Missing important baselines and comparisons: no direct privileged state supervision upper bound, limited diversity of SRL comparisons, teacher-student distillation underexplored in main paper

Under-justified design choices: proprioceptive vs privileged state split appears ad-hoc (Tables 2, 4); Equation 6's interval update mechanism feels orthogonal and like post-hoc fix; limited ablation on information allocation
Sample efficiency claims weakly supported: Figure 8 shows expected degradation with less data but true efficiency requires wall-clock time and computational budget analysis, which are underprovided
Presentation gaps: limited analysis of failure modes, unclear when PvP underperforms, weak explanation of why simpler VAE baseline performs well on motion imitation task
